newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cocoa price spike brings cash sellers to the fore.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa price spike brings cash sellers to the fore.

text.p: A sharp rise in cocoa futures this week has attracted sellers back into Europe's cash market but traders say industry is unlikely to buy in great quantity.

"There is some ammunition hitting the market at the moment," said one trader based in continental Europe. "The shippers who have been building up physical sales recently are looking at these sky-high prices."
London-traded cocoa futures have firmed considerably since the same time last week, when they dipped below 1,000 stg, basis the July position. On Thursday, July was trading close to 1,050.
Shippers were reportedly offering new crop Ivory at levels around 30 stg under the London terminal, with trade selling also seen about 10 stg above that.
It was not only Ivorian cocoa being offered, with traders noting Ghana as also being active in the market.
Traders said there was still some underlying demand for beans, primarily from German chocolate makers, but the price spike had probably deterred heavy fresh purchases.
"It's probably taken the wind out of their sails," one said.

Buyers were reported to have taken fresh cover last week, when prices were much lower, buying Ivorian and Nigerian beans for 1998 into 1999. Traders also said good quantities of butter were sold to Swiss and German chocolate manufacturers.
Traders pegged the latest price spike to rumours resurfacing over the state of the west African main crops, mentioning reports sourced to pod counters that all was not well.
"Don't forget it's the silly season and these rumours and counter-rumours are going around on a daily basis," one said.
There is also market concern over the possibility of drought in cocoa-producing regions of Africa, heightened by the development of an El Nino weather pattern in the south Pacific.
The last El Nino -- a warm water current which especially affects southern hemisphere rain patterns -- was in 1994/95, when scant rainfall fell in Africa but crop damage was minimal.
However, one trader pointed out that previous El Ninos had had a major affect on African rainfall and cocoa production.
"With all these fears in the market, it's probably wise to stay clear for a while -- and that's what I expect the physical trade in Europe to do," one said.

In the meantime, cocoa stocks in Europe have continued to decline, with SGS Warehouse Services estimating beans in store at the end of May at 569,000 tonnes in Amsterdam, down 40,000 on a month earlier.
